sections.overview: The common raccoon dog is a stocky member of the dog family, native to mainland East Asia. Its adaptable habits let it use woodland, wetlands, open country and some human-modified landscapes. Its dark facial mask gives the head a raccoon-like appearance, but its build and ancestry are canid. The species has also established far beyond its original Asian range after people released it for fur production in Europe.
sections.identification: Despite its name and dark eye mask, it is a canid, not a raccoon. Adults average about 56 cm in head-and-body length and roughly 4.5 kg, with local seasonal variation. A broad head, short legs and dense, shaggy coat give the animal a low, rounded outline; the dark mask contrasts with paler cheek fur. The tail is short and bushy, about 18 cm in one specialist account, and lacks the bold rings of a true raccoon. Winter fur grows longer and thicker, while moulting restores a shorter coat for warmer months. These dimensions describe wild adult reference samples, not a maximum: body mass changes substantially before and during winter rest.
sections.habitat: In its native range it occurs from China and Mongolia through Korea and the Russian Far East to northern Vietnam. Woodland edges, river valleys, scrub and wet ground offer cover beside varied feeding sites. Breeding adults use a den to raise their young.
sections.diet: This opportunistic omnivore shifts between plant foods and animal prey as local supplies change, and it also scavenges carrion. Estonian stomach samples illustrate the seasonal shift: autumn diets contained more amphibians and invertebrates, while winter samples held more small mammals, carrion and human-associated foods. Cereals and fruits at supplementary feeding sites, especially those for wild boar, supplied plant foods in that study.
sections.behavior: Raccoon dogs often form a breeding pair whose members use overlapping ranges and cooperate around the den. Field tracking in Germany found males guarding nursing pups while females made longer foraging trips. They are mainly active at night and around twilight, although local conditions and human disturbance can alter when they move. In southern Finland, tracked animals usually stayed in dens during midwinter but sometimes wandered even in the coldest months. In cold northern winters, individuals can enter long but intermittent bouts of reduced activity, rather than one uniform, deep hibernation.
sections.reproduction: In southern Finland, mating peaks in March; gestation lasts about 60–62 days, births are concentrated in May, and the mean litter at birth is about nine. Litter size and the proportion of females breeding vary with age, food and local conditions. Pups remain in a den for about six weeks, then begin travelling with their parents. Juveniles in Finland usually begin dispersing in August, with most leaving the natal range by September or October.
sections.ecology: In northern European wetlands, its predation can affect frogs and nesting waterbirds, although broad population effects remain difficult to establish. Local studies have found amphibians and bird eggs among its foods, so vulnerable island or shoreline breeding sites may face concentrated pressure. It also scavenges carcasses and competes with other medium-sized carnivores for this winter resource, though studies reviewed in Europe found little evidence of severe competition with foxes or badgers. In its introduced range, it can carry parasites and pathogens, making disease transmission an ecological and veterinary concern alongside predation.
sections.conservation: The global IUCN assessment, last assessed on 1 March 2016 and published in 2016, classified the raccoon dog taxon then recognized as Nyctereutes procyonoides as Least Concern with a stable trend; at that time it included Japanese populations now recognized separately by the Mammal Diversity Database. This historic category is not a new assessment of the current mainland species. Fur-farming releases in the former Soviet Union began a European expansion that continues to shape management. Between 1929 and 1955, about 9,100 animals were released in European Russia, and descendants spread into northern, eastern and central Europe. Its listing as an invasive alien species of Union concern applies from 2 February 2019. The current Union-list framework requires prevention or management measures. The main concerns are predation at sensitive local breeding sites and the spread of parasites and disease; evidence for continent-wide declines in native birds remains limited.
